The most plausible molecular mechanisms by which sexually dimorphic brain regions such as the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BSTc) and the third interstitial nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus (INAH3) develop along a trajectory distinct from the genitals involve the organizational effects of gonadal steroids and sex-chromosome-linked gene expression. During early gestation, testosterone from the fetal testes masculinizes the external genitalia, whereas brain sexual differentiation occurs later and continues into the second and early third trimesters. Testosterone and its aromatized metabolite estradiol act via androgen and estrogen receptors to modulate apoptosis, neuronal survival, synaptic patterning, and receptor density in hypothalamic and limbic circuits. Because the brain and genitals have different critical windows of sensitivity, variations in the timing, amplitude, or local metabolism of these hormones—due to placental aromatase activity, maternal stress, or endocrine-disrupting exposures—could produce a brain phenotype that is not concordant with somatic sex. Genetic influences also extend beyond SRY-mediated gonadal differentiation; X- and Y-linked genes such as *ZFY*, *NLGN4Y*, and *SRY* itself may be expressed in neural tissue and influence neural connectivity, while epigenetic modifications may further modulate hormone receptor expression in a region-specific manner.

Postmortem studies have reported that the volume and neuron number of the BSTc and INAH3 in transgender women resemble those typically observed in cisgender women rather than in cisgender men, whereas transgender men show patterns more consistent with cisgender men. These findings suggest that at least some neuroanatomical correlates of gender identity may be established prenatally through the same steroid-dependent pathways that organize other sexually dimorphic brain circuits. However, the evidence remains correlational and is based on small sample sizes, often with confounding factors such as hormone treatment history, sexual orientation, and age at death. Moreover, the functional significance of BSTc or INAH3 morphology for the subjective experience of gender identity is not fully understood; these structures are part of broader networks involving the hypothalamus, insula, and prefrontal cortex.

Consequently, while prenatal neuroendocrine and genetic mechanisms provide a biologically plausible foundation for brain–body discordance, they do not demonstrate that gender identity is rigidly “hardwired” before birth. The developing brain retains considerable plasticity, and gender identity is likely shaped by a dynamic interplay among prenatal biology, postnatal neurodevelopment, socialization, and lived experience. Thus, current evidence supports a predispositional rather than determinative model: early biological factors may canalize certain neural trajectories, but they do not fully predetermine gender identity. A nuanced interpretation recognizes that structural brain differences associated with gender identity are real and biologically grounded, yet they are best understood as one component of a complex, multifactorial developmental process rather than proof of immutable prenatal programming.

For Heidegger, technology is not merely a collection of instruments or a neutral means to human ends; it is, at bottom, a *mode of revealing* (*Weise des Entbergens*). In this sense, technology belongs to the history of truth because it determines how reality comes to presence for human beings. The Greek word *aletheia*—usually translated as “truth”—names the event of *unconcealment*, the process by which what was hidden comes into the open and can be encountered. Ancient *technē*, like *poiēsis*, was a form of “bringing-forth” (*Her-vor-bringen*): the craftsman or artist cooperated with nature to let things emerge into appearance. In this older dispensation, technology disclosed reality as something to be cared for and shaped, not simply dominated. Truth therefore precedes propositional correctness; it is the original clearing in which beings can show themselves as what they are.

Modern technology, however, reveals the real in a more aggressive and restrictive way. Rather than bringing forth, it “challenges forth” (*herausfordert*): nature is set upon, unlocked, transformed, and stored up as a calculable resource. A river is revealed not as a river but as a hydroelectric power source; a forest becomes cellulose, lumber, and oxygen yield. This mode of disclosure is what Heidegger calls *Gestell*, usually translated as “enframing.” *Gestell* is the essence of modern technology because it destines the real to appear everywhere as *Bestand*, “standing-reserve.” Human beings are not the autonomous masters of this process; they are themselves “started upon a way” of revealing by a *Geschick*, a destining or sending-that-gathers. Yet because humans are the site through whom this revealing occurs, technology remains a human way of disclosing truth—even if it is one that tends to reduce truth to the correctness of objectifying representation, the Roman *veritas* that measures things against a calculable order.

The connection between technology and truth is thus double-edged. On the one hand, modern technology makes reality accessible in unprecedented ways, turning the historical, the natural, and even human activity itself into objects for science, historiography, and administration. On the other hand, by revealing everything as standing-reserve, it conceals other possible ways of presencing and threatens to flatten the world into a stockpile of resources. Heidegger’s point is not that we should reject technology but that we must recognize it as a *destining* of revealing. Only by attending to the difference between technological disclosure and the more primordial *aletheia* can human beings recover a free relation to technology and allow truth to appear otherwise than as mere availability.

The central logical structure of Wiles’s argument is a proof by contradiction that converts Fermat’s Last Theorem into a statement about the modularity of elliptic curves. If there existed positive integers \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) and a prime exponent \(n>2\) satisfying \(a^n+b^n=c^n\), then the associated Frey curve  
\[
E_{a,b,c}: y^2=x(x-a^n)(x+b^n)
\]
would be a semistable elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{Q}\). Ribet’s theorem, building on the earlier work of Frey and Serre, shows that such a curve cannot be modular: its \(L\)-function would not correspond to any modular form. Consequently, establishing that every semistable elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{Q}\) is modular—i.e., that it is parametrized by a modular curve and its \(L\)-series is that of a weight-two cusp form—immediately rules out the hypothetical Frey curve and proves Fermat’s assertion.

Wiles attacks this modularity statement not by working directly with the curve, but with its \(p\)-adic Galois representations. For a prime \(p>3\), one considers the representation  
\[
\rho_{E,p^\infty}: G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}_p)
\]
on the Tate module, whose reduction modulo \(p\) is the residual representation  
\[
\rho_{E,p}: G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p).
\]
The key insight is a *modularity lifting theorem*: if the residual representation \(\rho_{E,p}\) is modular, then, under suitable hypotheses, the full \(p\)-adic representation \(\rho_{E,p^\infty}\) is also modular, and hence the curve \(E\) itself is modular. This reduces the problem to verifying modularity for a single residual representation. The difficulty is that knowing modularity modulo \(p\) only gives congruence information; one must lift it through all powers \(p^k\), which is precisely the *modular lifting problem*. Wiles solves it by embedding the problem in the deformation theory of Galois representations, comparing a universal deformation ring—which parametrizes all lifts of \(\rho_{E,p}\) with prescribed local behavior—to a Hecke algebra that parametrizes modular lifts.

The execution of this comparison depends on whether \(\rho_{E,p}\) is reducible or irreducible. When the residual representation is irreducible, Wiles uses the Taylor–Wiles patching method to prove that the universal deformation ring is isomorphic to the appropriate Hecke algebra, so every lift is modular. The reducible case is more delicate and is handled by auxiliary arguments, often by choosing a different prime where the representation becomes irreducible or by invoking the Langlands–Tunnell theorem for the \(3\)-adic case. Once modularity is established for at least one suitable prime, the lifting machinery propagates it to the whole curve, contradicting Ribet’s conclusion that the Frey curve is non-modular. Therefore no non-trivial solution to \(a^n+b^n=c^n\) with \(n>2\) can exist, and Fermat’s Last Theorem follows.

The most plausible neuroendocrine and genetic mechanisms through which sexually dimorphic hypothalamic and limbic structures—such as the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, central subdivision (BSTc) and the third interstitial nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus (INAH3)—could develop along a trajectory divergent from the genitals center on the organizational effects of gonadal steroids during discrete prenatal critical periods. According to the organizational–activational hypothesis, testosterone produced by the fetal testes during the second trimester is aromatized to estradiol in the brain and acts via estrogen receptors (ERα/ERβ) and androgen receptors (AR) to masculinize neural circuits, whereas the absence of a testosterone surge permits feminization in typical development. Because genital differentiation occurs earlier and relies partly on distinct downstream signaling cascades, a dissociation can arise if hormone exposure, receptor sensitivity, or local steroid metabolism differs between the genital ridge and the developing brain. Candidate mechanisms include polymorphisms in AR, CYP19A1 (aromatase), ESR1/ESR2, and SRD5A2; epigenetic programming of steroid-responsive genes; differential cell death, neurogenesis, and synaptic pruning; and direct chromosomal effects of X- and Y-linked genes such as *SRY* or *ZFY* that may influence neural patterning independently of circulating hormones. Prenatal environmental factors—maternal stress, immune activation, exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals, or altered placental steroid metabolism—may further modulate these pathways, producing a brain phenotype that is not concordant with the karyotypic or gonadal sex.

Whether such findings demonstrate that gender identity is “hardwired” before birth is far more contested. Postmortem studies have reported that the BSTc and INAH3 volumes in some transgender individuals resemble those typical of their experienced gender more than their birth-assigned sex, suggesting that at least some neural correlates of gender identity may be organized prenatally. However, these data are correlational, derived from small samples, and cannot establish causality; the same structures are also influenced by life history, hormones, and psychosocial factors across the lifespan. Moreover, “hardwired” is a misleading metaphor for neurodevelopment, which is probabilistic and experience-expectant rather than fixed. Brain sexual differentiation is a prolonged, multistage process, and discordance between genital and brain development is biologically plausible without implying that a specific gender identity is encoded in a single nucleus.

In sum, the developmental divergence of structures like the BSTc and INAH3 from the rest of the body can be explained by differential timing and local sensitivity to sex steroids, genetic variation, epigenetic modification, and prenatal environmental modulation. These mechanisms provide a strong biological foundation for understanding how gender identity could emerge independently of somatic sex characteristics. Nevertheless, current evidence supports a predisposition model rather than strict prenatal determinism: biology constrains and biases development, but gender identity is ultimately shaped by dynamic interactions among endocrine, genetic, neural, and social processes throughout life.

For Heidegger, technology is not merely a collection of instruments or a means to human ends; its essence lies in a particular mode of *revealing* (*Entbergen*). In this sense, technology is one of the ways in which beings come to appear—that is, one of the ways in which truth (*Wahrheit*) happens. The Greek word *aletheia*, usually translated as “truth,” originally names the event of *unconcealment*: the emergence of what is out of hiddenness into the open region of presence. Ancient *technē*, like poiesis, was a *bringing-forth* (*Her-vor-bringen*) that allowed what was latent in nature to come forward into appearance. Modern technology, by contrast, reveals the real through a *challenging-forth* (*Herausfordern*): it sets upon nature, unlocks, transforms, stores, and distributes it, so that the real shows up everywhere as *standing-reserve* (*Bestand*)—as calculable, disposable material awaiting use. Thus modern technology is a distinctive human path of disclosure: through it, reality is not simply encountered but is made to reveal itself as resource.

This modern mode of revealing is inseparable from the historical transformation of truth from Greek *aletheia* into Roman *veritas* and, eventually, into modern correctness of representation. *Aletheia* names the self-showing of beings in an open clearing; *veritas* and the later correspondence theory of truth already imply that beings are fixed as objects standing over against a representing subject. Modern technology intensifies this objectification: it frames the world as a field of measurable, manipulable objects, a framing Heidegger calls *Gestell* (enframing). The passage’s reference to historiography illustrates this point: history becomes accessible as an object for a science only because a prior *destining* (*Geschick*) has sent humanity into objectifying representation. The human being is therefore not the autonomous author of this revealing but the one who is *needed* and *claimed* by it, gathered into a way of disclosure that precedes and exceeds individual will.

Consequently, technology is a human way of revealing reality and bringing forth truth, but it is also a deeply ambiguous one. As a *sending-that-gathers*, it determines how beings can show themselves in a given epoch, and in the modern age it tends to reduce both nature and human beings themselves to standing-reserve. This totalizing disclosure conceals other possibilities of revealing—poetic, contemplative, or letting-be modes in which beings might appear otherwise. Yet because the essence of technology is a destining and not a fate, recognizing it as a mode of *aletheia* can open the possibility of a freer relation to it. In this way, technology remains a path of truth: it reveals the real, even as it challenges us to remember that revealing is never merely human production, but the event through which the world comes to presence.

Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem proceeds by reducing the arithmetic statement to a deep structural property of elliptic curves. One first supposes, for contradiction, that there exist positive integers \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) and a prime exponent \(n>2\) satisfying \(a^n+b^n=c^n\). From such a hypothetical solution, Frey observed that one can construct the semistable elliptic curve \(E_{a,b,c}: y^2=x(x-a^n)(x+b^n)\), now called the Frey curve. Ribet’s level-lowering theorem then shows that this curve, if it existed, would violate the Taniyama–Shimura–Weil conjecture: it would be a semistable elliptic curve over the rationals that is not modular. Consequently, proving that every semistable elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{Q}\) is modular is enough to rule out the hypothetical solution and establish Fermat’s Last Theorem.

The central innovation of Wiles is to attack modularity not by studying the curve directly, but by studying its associated Galois representations. For a prime \(p>3\), the \(p\)-torsion points of \(E\) give a two-dimensional mod-\(p\) Galois representation \(\rho(E,p)\). Wiles proves that if this single residual representation is modular—meaning it comes from a modular form—then the entire \(p\)-adic Tate module, and hence the elliptic curve \(E\) itself, must be modular. The difficulty is that modularity of the mod-\(p\) representation is a priori only a finite piece of information; one must “lift” it through all powers \(p^k\) to the full \(p\)-adic representation \(\rho(E,p^\infty)\). This is the modular lifting problem. Wiles solves it by interpreting Galois representations as deformations of the fixed residual representation and comparing the universal deformation ring \(R\), which parametrizes all such lifts, with a Hecke algebra \(T\), which parametrizes the modular ones. The equality \(R=T\), established via Taylor–Wiles patching, forces every lift to be modular.

The argument bifurcates according to whether \(\rho(E,p)\) is reducible or irreducible as a Galois module. The irreducible case is the heart of the proof and is handled by the Taylor–Wiles method for ordinary semistable representations. The reducible case, where the representation splits into one-dimensional characters, requires a separate deformation-theoretic analysis but is also covered by Wiles’s original work for semistable curves. Because one is free to choose any convenient prime \(p>3\), one can select a prime for which the residual representation is irreducible and ordinary, thereby putting oneself in the most favorable situation. Once the lifting theorem is in place, the Frey curve associated to a counterexample would have to be modular, contradicting Ribet’s result; hence no counterexample exists, and Fermat’s Last Theorem follows.

La diferenciación sexual del cerebro y de los genitales no ocurre de manera simultánea ni homogénea, lo que permite que estructuras como el núcleo central de la estría terminal (BSTc) y el tercer núcleo intersticial del hipotálamo anterior (INAH3) adopten características que no siempre coinciden con el sexo corporal. El mecanismo clásico descrito por Phoenix y cols. distingue entre efectos organizacionales —permanentes— y activacionales —reversibles— de las hormonas sexuales. Durante el desarrollo prenatal, el gen SRY del cromosoma Y desencadena la diferenciación testicular, cuyas células de Leydig producen testosterona. Esta hormona, mediante el receptor de andrógenos (AR), masculiniza los genitales externos aproximadamente entre las semanas 7 y 12 de gestación. Sin embargo, la diferenciación cerebral se extiende más allá del segundo trimestre e incluso al periodo perinatal. En el sistema nervioso central, la testosterona puede actuar directamente por AR o convertirse en estradiol mediante la aromatasa, activando los receptores de estrógenos (ERα y ERβ) para modelar circuitos hipotalámicos y límbicos. Además, hay evidencia de efectos directos de los cromosomas sexuales —genes ligados a X o Y, compensación de dosis, epigenética—, así como de factores ambientales como disruptores endocrinos, estrés materno, inmunización materna contra antígenos H-Y en embarazos masculinos sucesivos y condiciones placentarias. La asincronía entre estas ventanas de sensibilidad, sumada a la expresión local de enzimas y receptores en el hipotálamo, explicaría por qué estructuras como el BSTc o el INAH3 pueden seguir una trayectoria distinta a la del resto del cuerpo.

No obstante, que existan correlatos neuroanatómicos prenatales no demuestra de manera concluyente que la identidad de género esté “cableada” en el cerebro antes de nacer. Estudios post mortem, como los de Zhou y cols. (1995), Kruijver y cols. (2000) y García-Falgueras y Swaab (2008), han mostrado que el volumen y número de neuronas del BSTc en personas trans se asemejan más a su identidad de género que a su sexo asignado al nacer; de forma similar, investigaciones sobre el INAH3 han encontrado diferencias entre hombres gay, heterosexuales y mujeres, aunque con resultados heterogéneos. El problema metodológico central es que estas observaciones son correlacionales: no podemos saber si las diferencias estructurales son causa o consecuencia de la identidad, la orientación o las experiencias vividas. Además, el cerebro humano conserva una notable plasticidad durante toda la vida, por lo que factores postnatales —sociales, psicológicos y ambientales— también moldean la arquitectura neural. Por tanto, afirmar que la identidad de género está completamente predeterminada neurobiológicamente sería una simplificación excesiva.

En conjunto, el debate actual favorece un modelo biopsic social en el que factores neuroendocrinos y genéticos prenatales establecen predisposiciones, pero no destinos fijos. La metáfora del “cableado” resulta imprecisa porque sugiere un circuito rígido e inmutable, mientras que la neurociencia contemporánea describe un desarrollo probabilístico, sensible a múltiples niveles de influencia. Es necesario seguir investigando con diseños longitudinales, neuroimagen funcional y medidas hormonales prenatales para comprender mejor cómo interactúan la biología y el entorno en la configuración de la identidad de género. Lo que sí puede afirmarse con rigor es que el cerebro es una de las regiones donde la diferenciación sexual presenta una cronología y regulación particulares, lo que abre la puerta a trayectorias de desarrollo diversas sin que ello reduzca la identidad de género a una mera cuestión biológica predeterminada.

Below is a self-contained Python script. It vectorizes the ten French lines with character-level n-grams, computes pairwise cosine similarities, and reports the closest neighbor for each line (excluding the line itself).

```python
# nearest_neighbors_french.py
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
import numpy as np

corpus = [
    "D'où me vient ce désordre, Aufide, et que veut dire",
    "Madame, il était temps qu'il vous vînt du secours:",
    "Ah! Monsieur, c'est donc vous?",
    "Ami, j'ai beau rêver, toute ma rêverie",
    "Ne me parle plus tant de joie et d'hyménéé;",
    "Il est vrai, Cléobule, et je veux l'avouer",
    "Laisse-moi mon chagrin, tout injuste qu'il est;",
    "Ton frère, je l'avoue, a beacoup de mérite",
    "J'en demeure d'accord, chacun a sa méthode;",
    "Pour prix de votre amour que vous peignez extrême,",
]

# 1. Vectorize with character n-grams (including word boundaries)
vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
    analyzer="char_wb",      # character n-grams that include word edges
    ngram_range=(3, 5),      # overlapping sequences of 3 to 5 characters
    lowercase=True,          # case normalization
    sublinear_tf=True,       # dampen raw term frequencies
    use_idf=True             # down-weight n-grams common to many lines
)

X = vectorizer.fit_transform(corpus)

# 2. Compute pairwise cosine similarity
sim_matrix = cosine_similarity(X)

# 3. Find nearest neighbor for each line, excluding the line itself
np.fill_diagonal(sim_matrix, -1.0)  # prevent a line from matching itself
nearest_indices = sim_matrix.argmax(axis=1)
nearest_scores = sim_matrix[np.arange(len(corpus)), nearest_indices]

# 4. Display results
for i, text in enumerate(corpus):
    j = nearest_indices[i]
    print(f"Line {i}: {text}")
    print(f"  -> nearest neighbor is Line {j}: {corpus[j]}")
    print(f"  -> cosine similarity: {nearest_scores[i]:.4f}\n")
```

### Academic explanation

The script begins by transforming each short French line into a high-dimensional but sparse vector using character-level n-grams. An n-gram is a contiguous sequence of *n* characters extracted from a string; by setting `analyzer='char_wb'`, the vectorizer captures not only internal character sequences but also n-grams that straddle word boundaries, thereby encoding information about prefixes, suffixes, and short function words. For example, the line *“Ah! Monsieur, c'est donc vous?”* yields overlapping trigrams such as `ah!`, `! m`, ` mo`, `ons`, and so on. Because the corpus is small and literary, word-level tokenization would be brittle: lines are short, vocabulary overlap is limited, and spelling variants or archaic accents are common. Character n-grams instead create a dense local signature of orthography and morphology. The `TfidfVectorizer` then weights each n-gram by its term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) value, which emphasizes n-grams that are distinctive to a particular line while down-weighting those that appear in many lines. The result is a sparse matrix in which each row represents a text and each column represents one n-gram from the corpus vocabulary.

To compare these sparse vectors, the script uses cosine similarity, a metric that measures the cosine of the angle between two non-zero vectors. Mathematically, for two vectors **u** and **v**, cosine similarity is defined as  
\[
\cos(\theta)=\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|},
\]  
where the numerator is the dot product and the denominator is the product of the L2 norms. Because TF-IDF vectors contain only non-negative values, the score ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating identical n-gram distributions and 0 indicating no shared n-grams. Cosine similarity is especially appropriate for text because it is invariant to vector length: a long line and a short line can receive a high score if their relative n-gram distributions are similar. This is preferable to Euclidean distance in high-dimensional sparse spaces, where raw magnitude differences can dominate the measurement and obscure genuine distributional overlap.

Finally, the script constructs a full pairwise similarity matrix and retrieves the nearest neighbor for each line by selecting the column index with the maximum cosine score in each row. The diagonal entries, which would always be 1.0 because every line is perfectly similar to itself, are set to −1 so that the `argmax` operation returns the closest *other* line rather than the line itself. The output therefore maps each text to its most orthographically proximate counterpart in the corpus. It is worth noting that this approach captures surface-level lexical and graphemic similarity rather than deep semantic meaning; two lines may be nearest neighbors because they share pronouns, verbal endings, or punctuation patterns, not necessarily because they express related ideas. Adjusting the n-gram range or switching to word-level representations would alter the granularity of these comparisons.

Choice C is the provision that most clearly functions as an adhesive term and hides a material term of service. Website terms of service are the classic modern example of adhesion contracts: the operator drafts a single, standardized agreement, presents it to users on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, and the individual user has no realistic ability to negotiate. The clause at issue governs payment obligations and late charges—a quintessentially material term because it fixes the economic consequences of a user’s failure to pay. Because it is non-negotiable, one-sided, and inserted into a form contract, it bears all the hallmarks of an adhesive provision.

The deceptive language is found in the clause’s internal contradiction: it imposes “a late charge of one and one-half percent (10.5%) per month on the unpaid balance.” The spelled-out phrase “one and one-half percent” means 1.5% per month—an 18% annual rate that a reasonable consumer might expect for a late fee. The parenthetical “(10.5%)” is seven times larger and annualizes to a punitive 126% APR. By placing the higher figure in parentheses while spelling out the lower figure in words, the drafter creates a material ambiguity that obscures the true charge. A reasonable user skimming the agreement would likely rely on the written words and miss, or discount, the parenthetical. The drafter therefore had reason to believe that a user, if given the chance to bargain, would not accept a 126% late fee. That is precisely the circumstance the doctrine of reasonable expectations targets: a term is not enforceable when the party who wrote it knew or should have known the other party would not have assented to it.

Legally, the contradiction invites several remedies. Under the rule of *contra proferentem*, the ambiguity would be construed against the drafter, so a court could enforce only the 1.5% figure or strike the provision entirely. Alternatively, a 10.5% monthly charge could be deemed an unconscionable penalty or usurious interest, especially where it far exceeds the maximum rate allowed by law. The clause’s additional statement that “all Fees are non-refundable and payable in advance” further magnifies its one-sidedness. Because the true economic burden is hidden behind contradictory language, the term undermines informed consent and is the clearest example among the choices of an adhesion clause that hides a material term.

Below is a self-contained shell script that wraps Python so it can handle the enormous indices. It treats the Library of Babel as a finite combinatorial space: 25 symbols, 410 pages per book, 40 lines per page, and 80 characters per line. The input is a single non-negative decimal integer that uniquely identifies a page among all pages in the library.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# library_of_babel.sh
# Deterministically generate one page of Borges's Library of Babel.
# Usage: ./library_of_babel.sh <page_index> [--oneline]
#
# The page_index is a single decimal integer that enumerates every page.
# If you already have a book index b and a page number p (0-409),
# use N = 410*b + p.

exec python3 - "$@" <<'PY'
import sys

# Python 3.11+ limits int<->str conversions by default; disable the limit
# so we can parse indices with millions of decimal digits.
if hasattr(sys, "set_int_max_str_digits"):
    sys.set_int_max_str_digits(0)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Library parameters
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# 25 symbols: 22 letters + period + comma + space.
# (The excerpt you supplied uses the common 29-symbol web convention:
# a-z + ., + space.  To use that version, change ALPHABET to 29 chars.)
ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuv., "   # 25 characters; last is space
BASE = len(ALPHABET)                     # 25

LINES_PER_PAGE = 40
CHARS_PER_LINE = 80
CHARS_PER_PAGE = LINES_PER_PAGE * CHARS_PER_LINE   # 3,200
PAGES_PER_BOOK = 410
CHARS_PER_BOOK = CHARS_PER_PAGE * PAGES_PER_BOOK   # 1,312,000

# Total pages in the finite library: 410 * 25^1,312,000
MAX_PAGES = PAGES_PER_BOOK * pow(BASE, CHARS_PER_BOOK)


def generate_page(book_index: int, page_num: int) -> str:
    """Return the requested page as a string of CHARS_PER_PAGE symbols."""
    if not (0 <= page_num < PAGES_PER_BOOK):
        raise ValueError(f"page number must be in [0, {PAGES_PER_BOOK - 1}]")

    # The page starts at character offset k = page_num * CHARS_PER_PAGE.

    chars = []
    for _ in range(CHARS_PER_PAGE):
        x, digit = divmod(x, BASE)
        chars.append(ALPHABET[digit])
```

### Mathematical combinatorics and indexing logic

In Jorge Luis Borges’s *La Biblioteca de Babel*, the library becomes a finite combinatorial object once its alphabet and format are fixed. The implementation assumes the dimensions usually inferred from the story: each book contains 410 pages, each page contains 40 lines, and each line contains 80 characters. Consequently, a page is a string of 3,200 symbols and a book is a string of 1,312,000 symbols. With an alphabet of 25 characters, the multiplication principle gives \(25^{1,312,000}\) possible books and \(410 \times 25^{1,312,000}\) possible pages. Although these numbers are astronomically larger than any physical collection, they are finite cardinals, so the pages can be placed in a one-to-one correspondence with the non-negative integers.

The script realizes this correspondence by treating the input index \(N\) as a mixed-radix coordinate. First, Euclidean division separates the book index \(b\) and the page number \(p\): \(N = 410b + p\), with \(b = \lfloor N/410 \rfloor\) and \(p = N \bmod 410\). The book index \(b\) is then read as a 1,312,000-digit base-25 numeral, where the least significant digit corresponds to the first character of the book and the most significant digit to the last. A fixed lookup table maps the digits \(0,\dots,24\) onto the 25 symbols—here the first 22 lowercase letters followed by the period, comma, and space. Because every integer in the range \([0, 25^{1,312,000} - 1]\) has a unique base-25 expansion of exactly that length when leading zeros are allowed, this step is a bijection between book indices and books.

To retrieve only the requested page, the script avoids materializing the entire book. If page \(p\) begins at character offset \(k = p \cdot 3{,}200\), it computes \(x = b \,//\, 25^{k}\), which shifts the desired block into the least-significant positions, and then extracts 3,200 consecutive digits by repeatedly applying \(\operatorname{divmod}(x, 25)\). Each digit is translated through the lookup table, and the resulting characters are printed as 40 lines of 80 characters. Python’s arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic makes this practical even when \(N\) contains millions of decimal digits, because the intermediate values are never larger than the index itself. The procedure contains no randomness, so the mapping is strictly deterministic: identical indices always produce identical pages, converting Borges’s labyrinth into a computable enumeration.

Below is a self-contained Python script that integrates the Lorenz system with a hand-written 4th-order Runge–Kutta (RK4) scheme, evolves two nearby initial conditions, and computes their Euclidean separation over time. The script uses only NumPy for the integration and Matplotlib for visualization.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Self-contained RK4 integration of the Lorenz system.
Demonstrates sensitivity to initial conditions by comparing two
trajectories whose initial x-coordinates differ by 1e-4.
"""

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def lorenz(t, state, sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8.0 / 3.0):
    """
    Right-hand side of the Lorenz system.
    state = [x, y, z]
    """
    x, y, z = state
    dx = sigma * (y - x)
    dy = x * (rho - z) - y
    dz = x * y - beta * z
    return np.array([dx, dy, dz], dtype=float)


def rk4_step(f, t, y, h, *params):
    """
    One step of the classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta method.
    """
    k1 = f(t, y, *params)
    k2 = f(t + h / 2.0, y + h * k1 / 2.0, *params)
    k3 = f(t + h / 2.0, y + h * k2 / 2.0, *params)
    k4 = f(t + h, y + h * k3, *params)
    return y + (h / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)


def integrate_rk4(f, y0, t_span, h, *params):
    """
    Integrate dy/dt = f(t, y) from t_span[0] to t_span[1] with step size h.
    Returns arrays t and y, where y[i] is the state at time t[i].
    """
    t0, tf = t_span
    n_steps = int(np.ceil((tf - t0) / h))
    # Adjust h so that the final time is hit exactly.
    h = (tf - t0) / n_steps
    t = np.linspace(t0, tf, n_steps + 1)
    y = np.zeros((n_steps + 1, len(y0)), dtype=float)
    y[0] = y0

    for i in range(n_steps):
        y[i + 1] = rk4_step(f, t[i], y[i], h, *params)

    return t, y


def main():
    # Standard Lorenz parameters
    sigma, rho, beta = 10.0, 28.0, 8.0 / 3.0

    # Two nearby initial conditions
    y0_A = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], dtype=float)
    y0_B = np.array([1.0001, 1.0, 1.0], dtype=float)

    t_span = (0.0, 40.0)
    h = 0.001

    # Integrate both trajectories
    t, traj_A = integrate_rk4(lorenz, y0_A, t_span, h, sigma, rho, beta)
    _, traj_B = integrate_rk4(lorenz, y0_B, t_span, h, sigma, rho, beta)

    # Euclidean distance between the two trajectories over time
    distance = np.linalg.norm(traj_A - traj_B, axis=1)

    print(f"Initial separation: {distance[0]:.6e}")
    print(f"Final separation at t = {t[-1]:.2f}: {distance[-1]:.6e}")

    # Estimate the maximal Lyapunov exponent from the early exponential-growth
    # regime, before the separation saturates at the attractor size.
    mask = (t > 2.0) & (t < 12.0)
    if np.any(distance[mask] > 0.0):
        slope, intercept = np.polyfit(t[mask], np.log(distance[mask]), 1)
        print(f"Estimated maximal Lyapunov exponent (t = 2..12): {slope:.4f}")

    # Plot the two x(t) time series and the separation on a log scale
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

    axes[0].plot(t, traj_A[:, 0], label=r"$x_A(t)$")
    axes[0].plot(t, traj_B[:, 0], "--", label=r"$x_B(t)$")
    axes[0].set_xlabel("Time $t$")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("$x(t)$")
    axes[0].set_title("Lorenz $x(t)$ for two nearby initial conditions")
    axes[0].legend()

    axes[1].semilogy(t, distance, color="crimson")
    axes[1].set_xlabel("Time $t$")
    axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\|\mathbf{x}_A(t) - \mathbf{x}_B(t)\|_2$")
    axes[1].set_title("Euclidean separation between trajectories")

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

The Lorenz attractor is the canonical example of a *strange attractor*: a bounded, invariant set in three-dimensional phase space on which the dynamics are chaotic. Geometrically, it resembles a pair of butterfly wings, with two lobes centered on the unstable spiral fixed points \(C_\pm=(\pm\sqrt{\beta(\rho-1)},\pm\sqrt{\beta(\rho-1)},\rho-1)\). A trajectory spirals outward within one lobe, then is reinjected across to the other lobe in an apparently unpredictable sequence. Although each trajectory is smooth and deterministic, the attractor itself has a fractal structure—its capacity dimension is approximately \(2.06\)—reflecting the repeated stretching and folding that creates a Cantor-like layering of surfaces. Despite this complexity, phase-space volumes contract because the divergence of the Lorenz vector field is the negative constant \(-(\sigma+1+\beta)\); thus the attractor occupies zero volume and can be thought of as a thin, folded sheet embedded in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

Phase-space trajectories of the Lorenz system illustrate the hallmark of deterministic chaos: *sensitivity to initial conditions*. Because the flow is governed by a smooth ordinary differential equation, any two infinitesimally close points initially remain close for a short time, but their separation grows roughly as \(\|\delta(t)\| \sim \|\delta(0)\|e^{\lambda_{\max} t}\) with \(\lambda_{\max}>0\). This exponential divergence means that microscopic uncertainties are amplified to macroscopic scales within a characteristic predictability time of order \(1/\lambda_{\max}\). At the same time, the trajectories remain confined to the attractor, so the separation eventually saturates near the attractor’s diameter. The resulting motion is aperiodic, bounded, and mixing: the system explores the attractor in a non-repeating fashion, making long-term prediction impossible even though the governing equations contain no stochastic terms.

The *maximal Lyapunov exponent* quantifies this average rate of separation. For a deterministic flow \(\Phi^t\) generated by \(\dot{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\), let \(\delta(t)=\mathbf{x}(t)-\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(t)\) be the infinitesimal displacement between two nearby trajectories. The maximal Lyapunov exponent is defined by

\[
\lambda_{\max}
=
\lim_{t\to\infty}
\lim_{\|\delta(0)\|\to 0}
\frac{1}{t}
\ln\frac{\|\delta(t)\|}{\|\delta(0)\|}.
\]

Equivalently, through the multiplicative ergodic theorem of Oseledets, it can be expressed in terms of the linearized dynamics as

\[
\lambda_{\max}
=
\lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{1}{t}
\ln\|D\Phi^t(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{v}\|,
\]

for a typical initial point \(\mathbf{x}\) and a typical tangent vector \(\mathbf{v}\). A positive \(\lambda_{\max}\) indicates chaos: nearby states diverge on average. A zero exponent corresponds to a neutral direction, and a negative exponent signals contraction or stability. For the standard Lorenz parameters \(\sigma=10\), \(\beta=8/3\), and \(\rho=28\), the maximal Lyapunov exponent is approximately \(0.90\), meaning that small perturbations grow by a factor of roughly \(e^{0.90}\approx 2.46\) per unit time, thereby setting the fundamental predictability horizon of the system.

```python
"""
Lorenz system RK4 integration and sensitivity to initial conditions.
Dependencies: numpy, matplotlib
"""

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def lorenz(t, state, sigma=10.0, beta=8.0 / 3.0, rho=28.0):
    """
    Right-hand side of the Lorenz system.
    state = [x, y, z]
    """
    x, y, z = state
    dx = sigma * (y - x)
    dy = x * (rho - z) - y
    dz = x * y - beta * z
    return np.array([dx, dy, dz], dtype=float)


def rk4_step(f, t, y, h, *args):
    """
    One step of the classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method.
    """
    k1 = f(t, y, *args)
    k2 = f(t + h / 2.0, y + h * k1 / 2.0, *args)
    k3 = f(t + h / 2.0, y + h * k2 / 2.0, *args)
    k4 = f(t + h, y + h * k3, *args)
    return y + h * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4) / 6.0


def integrate_rk4(f, y0, t_span, h, *args):
    """
    Fixed-step RK4 integration from t_span[0] to t_span[1].
    Returns time array and solution array of shape (n_steps+1, len(y0)).
    """
    t0, tf = t_span
    n_steps = int(np.round((tf - t0) / h))
    h = (tf - t0) / n_steps  # adjust h to land exactly on tf

    ts = np.linspace(t0, tf, n_steps + 1)
    ys = np.zeros((n_steps + 1, len(y0)), dtype=float)
    ys[0] = y0
    y = y0.astype(float).copy()

    for i in range(n_steps):
        y = rk4_step(f, ts[i], y, h, *args)
        ys[i + 1] = y

    return ts, ys


if __name__ == "__main__":
```

### Academic explanation

The Lorenz attractor is the canonical example of a **strange attractor**: a bounded, invariant set in three-dimensional phase space that has a fractal geometric structure and supports complicated, aperiodic dynamics. For the standard parameters \(\sigma=10\), \(\beta=8/3\), and \(\rho=28\), the attractor has the familiar “butterfly” shape, organized around two unstable fixed points located at \(C_{\pm}=(\pm\sqrt{\beta(\rho-1)},\pm\sqrt{\beta(\rho-1)},\rho-1)\). A trajectory spirals outward from one lobe, then is injected into the other, repeating this process indefinitely without ever following a closed orbit. Although the attractor occupies a finite region of phase space, its cross-sections display a Cantor-set-like layering, and its Hausdorff dimension is approximately \(2.06\), intermediate between a smooth surface and a volume-filling object. This fractal geometry arises from the competing actions of stretching, which separates nearby points, and folding, which keeps trajectories confined and prevents them from diverging to infinity.

In phase-space terms, the Lorenz system defines a deterministic flow \(\phi_t:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3\) that maps an initial condition \(\mathbf{x}_0\) to its state \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) at time \(t\). Because the equations are smooth and autonomous, the flow is unique and differentiable, so every trajectory is completely determined by its starting point. Nevertheless, the flow is **sensitively dependent on initial conditions**: two states that begin arbitrarily close together are rapidly pulled apart as they evolve. The script above quantifies this by integrating two trajectories whose initial \(x\)-coordinates differ by only \(10^{-4}\) and computing the Euclidean distance \(\|\mathbf{x}_A(t)-\mathbf{x}_B(t)\|_2\) at each time step. Initially this distance grows exponentially, reflecting the instability of the attractor, before eventually saturating at a value comparable to the attractor’s diameter. This behavior is the hallmark of deterministic chaos: the system is perfectly predictable in principle, yet long-term forecasting is impossible in practice because any finite measurement or numerical error is amplified.

The rate at which infinitesimally close trajectories separate is captured by the **maximal Lyapunov exponent** (MLE), denoted \(\lambda_{\max}\). Mathematically, let \(\boldsymbol{\delta}(t)=\mathbf{x}(t)-\mathbf{x}'(t)\) be the separation vector between two trajectories starting from \(\mathbf{x}_0\) and \(\mathbf{x}_0+\boldsymbol{\delta}_0\). For small perturbations, the norm typically obeys \(\|\boldsymbol{\delta}(t)\|\sim\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_0\|e^{\lambda_{\max} t}\), and the MLE is defined by the double limit

\[
\lambda_{\max}
=
\lim_{t\to\infty}
\lim_{\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_0\|\to 0}
\frac{1}{t}
\ln\frac{\|\boldsymbol{\delta}(t)\|}{\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_0\|}.
\]

A positive \(\lambda_{\max}\) indicates exponential divergence of nearby trajectories and is the standard diagnostic for chaos; a zero exponent corresponds to marginal stability, while a negative exponent signals convergence. For the standard Lorenz system, \(\lambda_{\max}\approx 0.905\), meaning that small errors grow by a factor of roughly \(e^{0.905}\approx 2.47\) per unit time. In numerical practice, the MLE is estimated by repeatedly renormalizing a small perturbation vector so that it remains infinitesimal, because an unrenormalized perturbation will eventually grow to the size of the attractor and the exponential rate will be lost.

### Academic explanation

Circular topological fingerprints, exemplified by the Extended Connectivity Fingerprint (ECFP) family, encode a molecule as a collection of overlapping atom-centered substructures rather than as a fixed structural key. The algorithm begins by assigning each atom an initial identifier that compresses invariant local properties—atomic number, connectivity degree, formal charge, aromaticity, and hybridization state—into a compact integer. In each subsequent iteration, an atom’s identifier is updated by hashing a sorted tuple composed of its own current identifier together with the identifiers of its directly bonded neighbors. Because this update propagates outward by one bond per iteration, a fingerprint generated after *r* iterations captures all circular environments of radius *r* around every atom. ECFP4, for instance, uses a radius of two bonds and therefore records substructures with a diameter of up to four bonds. The resulting integer hashes are collected and, in the common bit-vector implementation, folded modulo a fixed length such as 1024 or 2048 bits. This folding introduces a controlled possibility of bit collisions but yields a uniform, machine-readable representation that is invariant to atom numbering and highly sensitive to local chemical topology.

The Tanimoto coefficient, also called the Jaccard index, quantifies the overlap between two binary fingerprints. If **A** and **B** are bit vectors, let *a* be the number of bits set in **A**, *b* the number set in **B**, and *c* the number set in both. The similarity is defined as

\[
T(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})=\frac{|\mathbf{A}\cap\mathbf{B}|}{|\mathbf{A}\cup\mathbf{B}|}=\frac{c}{a+b-c},
\]

which ranges from 0 for no shared features to 1 for identical fingerprints. The corresponding Tanimoto distance is simply \(D = 1 - T\). Because ECFP bit vectors are sparse, the expected background similarity between two unrelated molecules is approximately the square of the bit density, so even modest positive values can reflect genuine structural relationships rather than random overlap.

In modern virtual screening and medicinal chemistry, Tanimoto similarities are interpreted through the lens of the similarity–property principle: structurally similar molecules tend to share biological activities, physicochemical properties, and toxicological profiles. For ECFP4 fingerprints, a Tanimoto value above 0.7–0.85 often signals a shared scaffold or pharmacophore and is frequently used as a cutoff for retrieving analogs from large chemical libraries. Values between 0.3 and 0.5 usually represent background chemical similarity, whereas values below 0.3 indicate largely distinct chemotypes. Nevertheless, these thresholds are heuristic; “activity cliffs” can occur where small structural changes abolish or enhance potency, and highly similar molecules can differ dramatically in ADMET behavior. Consequently, similarity scores are now commonly integrated with machine-learning models, docking, and experimental validation rather than used as standalone decision criteria.

### Academic explanation

The **Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)** is the mathematical bridge between a signal’s time-domain representation and its frequency-domain representation. For a finite sequence of \(N\) samples \(x[n]\), the DFT is defined as  
\[
X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]\,e^{-i2\pi kn/N},
\]  
where each bin \(k\) corresponds to a complex sinusoid at frequency \(f_k=k f_s/N\). By projecting the signal onto this orthogonal basis of complex exponentials, the DFT decomposes the waveform into a set of sinusoidal components, each characterized by a magnitude and a phase. The **Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)** is merely an efficient algorithm for computing the DFT in \(O(N\log N)\) operations rather than the naïve \(O(N^2)\). For real-valued audio signals, the spectrum is conjugate-symmetric, so analysis is typically restricted to the positive frequencies from DC up to the Nyquist frequency \(f_s/2\), with a frequency resolution of \(\Delta f = f_s/N = 1/T\) for a signal of duration \(T\) seconds.

The perceived **timbre** of a musical tone—what allows a piano, violin, and flute playing the same pitch to sound distinct—is determined primarily by the static and time-varying structure of the harmonic spectrum. A periodic tone can be modeled as a sum of a fundamental frequency \(f_0\) and integer overtones \(2f_0, 3f_0, \dots\), whose relative amplitudes form a spectral envelope. The auditory system performs a quasi-frequency analysis along the basilar membrane, and when harmonics are present in integer ratios, the brain fuses them into a single pitch sensation; this is the basis of the **missing fundamental** phenomenon. Brighter or more “nasal” timbres generally contain stronger energy in higher harmonics, whereas mellow timbres are dominated by lower partials. In the synthesized C-major triad above, adding the second and third harmonics at logarithmically decaying amplitudes transforms the sterile sound of pure sine waves into a richer, more instrument-like sonority.

A fundamental constraint governing all such time-frequency analysis is the **time-frequency uncertainty principle**, often called the **Gabor limit**. It states that the product of a signal’s temporal spread \(\sigma_t\) and its spectral spread \(\sigma_f\) is bounded below by a constant,  
\[
\sigma_t\,\sigma_f \ge \frac{1}{4\pi}.
\]  
In practical DSP terms, this means that improving frequency resolution requires a longer observation window, while improving temporal resolution requires a shorter window; the two cannot be optimized simultaneously. For a one-second recording at 44.1 kHz, the FFT bin width is 1 Hz, so closely spaced frequencies can be resolved only if they differ by roughly this amount or more. This trade-off pervades short-time Fourier transforms, spectrograms, and pitch-tracking algorithms, reminding us that any representation of sound is necessarily a compromise between knowing *when* a spectral event occurs and knowing *exactly what frequency* it contains.

```python
import random
import time


class SegmentTree:
    """
    Iterative segment tree for range-sum / point-update.
    The tree is stored in a flat list of size 2 * size,
    where size is the next power of two >= n.
    """

    def __init__(self, data):
        self.n = len(data)
        self.size = 1
        while self.size < self.n:
            self.size <<= 1

        self.tree = [0] * (2 * self.size)

        # leaves
        for i in range(self.n):
            self.tree[self.size + i] = data[i]

        # internal nodes
        for i in range(self.size - 1, 0, -1):
            self.tree[i] = self.tree[2 * i] + self.tree[2 * i + 1]

    def update(self, idx, value):
        """Point update: set data[idx] = value."""
        pos = self.size + idx
        self.tree[pos] = value
        pos >>= 1
        while pos:
            self.tree[pos] = self.tree[2 * pos] + self.tree[2 * pos + 1]
            pos >>= 1

    def query(self, l, r):
        """
        Range sum query on the inclusive interval [l, r].
        Internally converted to the half-open interval [l, r+1).
        """
        l += self.size
        r += self.size + 1
        res = 0
        while l < r:
            if l & 1:
                res += self.tree[l]
                l += 1
            if r & 1:
                r -= 1
                res += self.tree[r]
            l >>= 1
            r >>= 1
        return res


def test_correctness(trials=200):
    """Small randomized test to verify the segment tree against a naive array."""
    for n in [1, 5, 17, 100, 255]:
        arr = [random.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(n)]
        st = SegmentTree(arr)
        for _ in range(trials):
            if random.random() < 0.5:
                i = random.randrange(n)
                v = random.randint(-100, 100)
                arr[i] = v
                st.update(i, v)
            else:
                l = random.randrange(n)
                r = random.randrange(l, n)
                expected = sum(arr[l:r + 1])
                got = st.query(l, r)
                assert expected == got, f"mismatch at [{l},{r}]: {expected} != {got}"
    print("Correctness tests passed.")


def benchmark(N=100_000, Q=50_000, seed=0):
    random.seed(seed)

    # synthetic dataset
    data = [random.randint(0, 1000) for _ in range(N)]

    # generate the same intermixed operation sequence for both structures
    ops = []
    for _ in range(Q):
        if random.random() < 0.5:
            ops.append(("u", random.randrange(N), random.randint(0, 1000)))
        else:
            l = random.randrange(N)
            r = random.randrange(l, N)
            ops.append(("q", l, r))

    num_updates = sum(1 for op in ops if op[0] == "u")
    num_queries = Q - num_updates

    # --- naive continuous array ---
    naive = data[:]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for op in ops:
        if op[0] == "u":
            naive[op[1]] = op[2]
        else:
            _ = sum(naive[op[1]:op[2] + 1])
    t_naive = time.perf_counter() - t0

    # --- segment tree ---
    st = SegmentTree(data)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for op in ops:
        if op[0] == "u":
            st.update(op[1], op[2])
        else:
            _ = st.query(op[1], op[2])
    t_st = time.perf_counter() - t0

    print(f"\nBenchmark: N = {N:,}, Q = {Q:,}")
    print(f"Updates: {num_updates:,}, Range-sum queries: {num_queries:,}")
    print(f"Naive array time:   {t_naive:.4f} s")
    print(f"Segment tree time:  {t_st:.4f} s")
    if t_st > 0:
        print(f"Speedup:            {t_naive / t_st:.2f}x")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_correctness()
    benchmark()
```

### Academic Complexity Analysis

The dynamic range-sum with point-update problem admits two conceptually different representations. In the **naive contiguous-array strategy**, the underlying array is stored verbatim; a point update therefore costs Θ(1) time, but a range sum over *k* elements costs Θ(k). In the worst case *k* = Θ(N), so *Q* intermixed operations can cost Θ(NQ) time, while the space consumption is Θ(N). By contrast, a **balanced segment tree** stores aggregate sums over recursively halved intervals. Its construction visits every leaf and every internal node exactly once, giving Θ(N) time and Θ(N) auxiliary space. Each point update propagates from a leaf to the root, and each range query decomposes the requested interval into at most two nodes per tree level. Consequently, both operations are Θ(log N) in the worst, best, and average cases—formally, O(log N), Ω(log N), and therefore Θ(log N).

Formally, let *T*<sub>c</sub>(*N*) denote the construction cost for *N* elements. Because the tree recursively splits the interval into two halves and performs Θ(1) work to combine the children, the recurrence is *T*<sub>c</sub>(*N*) = 2*T*<sub>c</sub>(*N*/2) + Θ(1) with *T*<sub>c</sub>(1) = Θ(1). By the Master Theorem, since *a* = 2, *b* = 2, and *f*(*N*) = Θ(1) = *O*(*N*<sup>1−ε</sup>), the solution is *T*<sub>c</sub>(*N*) = Θ(*N*). For traversal, let *T*<sub>t</sub>(*N*) be the cost of a query or update. At each step the relevant subproblem size halves while only Θ(1) nodes are processed, so *T*<sub>t</sub>(*N*) = *T*<sub>t</sub>(*N*/2) + Θ(1), which solves to Θ(log *N*). The *O*(log *N*) height bound follows directly from the splitting process: after *h* levels the interval length is at most *N*/2<sup>*h*</sup>, and the recursion terminates when *N*/2<sup>*h*</sup> ≤ 1, i.e., *h* ≥ log₂*N*. Rounding up to the next power of two yields height *h* = ⌈log₂*N*⌉ = Θ(log *N*). Because each level contributes only constant work per visited node and at most two nodes per level are visited, query and update costs are tightly bounded by Θ(log *N*).

Nevertheless, asymptotic efficiency does not tell the whole story once physical hardware is considered. The naive array enjoys excellent spatial locality: a range sum scans contiguous memory, maximizing cache-line utilization and CPU prefetching; when the summation loop is executed in optimized C code, its per-operation constant is very small. The segment tree, although asymptotically faster, stores up to 4*N* aggregate values and accesses memory with strides that halve at each level, which can reduce cache locality and increase misses. For small *N* or very short query ranges, the naive method may even outperform the segment tree because its Θ(*N*) cost is hidden by low constant factors and superior cache behavior. As *N* and the number of queries grow, however, the asymptotic gap dominates: Θ(*NQ*) versus Θ(*Q* log *N*). Thus Big-O notation correctly identifies the scalable winner, but constants, memory footprint, and cache hierarchy determine the practical crossover point.
